**Surah al-Haaqqa**

Its purpose is to declare God free of imperfection through the resurrection of creatures, so that truth is established and falsehood is destroyed, by a complete disclosure that results from the all-encompassing reach of His knowledge over universals and particulars, and from the perfect power He has over the higher and lower realms, and by manifesting justice among all created beings. This is so that the Muslim may be distinguished from the criminal through what delights and what pains. Its name, al-Haaqqa, is most clearly suited to this, and it is the most indicative of this purpose among its features. (In the name of God, to whom belongs all perfection, in exalting Him and praising Him; the All-Merciful, whose generosity has encompassed all through justice, in greatness and glory; the Ever-Merciful, who has singled out the people of His friendship by standing at His limits, so that they may attain, through the goodness of His nearness, exaltation, fortune, the fulfilment of hopes and felicity.)

* *

When He, glory be to Him, had in "Nun" (Surah al-Qalam) presented the severe denial that the evildoer be made equal to the good-doer, and had mentioned the Resurrection and explained it by the Day of the disclosure of the shin (saq) and the increase of hardships, and had threatened with a great threat through the verse of *istidraj* (gradual enticement, the process by which one is led on step by step to ruin), which cannot be averted by any remedy, and concluded that the Qur'an is a *dhikr* (a reminder, i.e. honour) and an admonition, and admonitions for all the worlds in their entirety (p-338) by His mercy, then after its revelation it is by His threat, His promise, His exhortation, His narratives, His command and His prohibition; and before its revelation it is by bearing witness for them and against them. The interpretation (*ta'wil*) of all that and all its effects only becomes fully manifest on the Day of the Great Gathering. That day is the greatest reminder, admonition and deterrent for all the worlds, upon remembering which all good is founded, and upon remembering the presentation before the Sovereign, the Judge. The secret of the revelation of the Qur'an is the reminder of that Day, which is the order of existence. He said, describing the Resurrection and the Day on which the shin is disclosed, admonishing by mentioning it and warning about its matter:

﴿The Inevitable Reality﴾ [i.e.] the Hour by which these people deny, and it is the most established and most manifest of things. There is no falsehood in it, nor anything false about it. It must necessarily come to its rights, for it is firm in itself, and the matters in it are presented in their realities, and recompense is given for them according to the truth about which there is no doubt for any of creation. Thus it is an active participle (*fa'ila*) in the sense of a passive (*maf'ul*), since things are done in it. It is also an active participle because it overcomes every adversary, from *haqaqtuhu fa-haqqaqtuhu uhiquhu*, meaning I contended with him over the truth and prevailed over him in it. So it makes the truth prevail without fail, and it rises above falsehood, crushing and destroying it. Thus it makes the punishment due to the criminals and the reward due to the Muslims. Everything in it rests on firmness and clarity, because that is what wisdom requires. No ruler would accept leaving his subjects without establishing justice between them according to his own claim, so how much more so the Wise, the All-Knowing. The story of the companion of the fish, upon him be peace, is the clearest proof of His power over these matters.

When all of that was a matter that astonishes the intellects, shakes the hearts, and disturbs the souls, and when the coarse, rough-natured person might perhaps hesitate about it, He emphasized its matter, increased its awfulness, and went to great lengths in magnifying and exalting it, indicating that its terror escapes description by [His] saying, informing that it is among the things that rightly warrant asking about it, driving it forward with the interrogative particle, intending by it the magnification of the matter, and that news is not like seeing with one's own eyes: ﴿What is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ So the interrogative particle is a subject (mubtada'), about which the predicate is given as "the Inevitable Reality" (al-Haqqah), and these two together form a predicate for the first (the interrogative particle). The linking element is the repetition of the subject with its own wording, as in "Zayd, i.e., what is he"; and this is most common when the meaning of magnification and awe is intended.

Since the context concerns conveying the matter through "the uncovering of the shin" (kashf al-saq), the awe is magnified by His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Reality is?﴾ meaning, in the past tense, and He shortened it so that the soul may roam in it in every direction: that is, what could inform you of anything among things, even with your engagement in inquiry and deliberation? Then the warning about it increased by His saying, in the first manner, in interrogative form, and the purpose of it is exaltation and further magnification: ﴿What is the Reality?﴾ That is, it is of such a nature (p-340) that no one knows its true nature, nor does it reach it, nor does his understanding attain it, and however its state is estimated, it is greater than that; so it is not known with true knowledge except by direct witnessing.

Imam Abu Ja'far Ibn al-Zubayr said: When Surat "Nun, wal-Qalam" [al-Qalam: 1] was built upon the rebuke and reproof of the polytheists of Quraysh and the rest of the Arabs, and the declaration of the Prophet of Allah ﷺ free from their monstrous speech and foul slander, and (it mentioned) their envy and hostility: ﴿And indeed, those who disbelieve would almost slip you with their eyes﴾ [al-Qalam: 51], it was followed by Surat al-Haqqah as a promise to them and an explanation that their condition in the evil of that deed had already been preceded by others: ﴿Thamud and 'Ad denied the Striking Calamity﴾ [al-Haqqah: 4], ﴿So do you see any remnant of them?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 8] [﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ [al-An'am: 6], ﴿Do they await except the like of the days of those who passed before them?﴾ [Yunus: 102]], and ﴿And how many generations We destroyed before them. Do you perceive any of them, or hear from them a whisper?﴾ [Maryam: 98]. So Surat al-Haqqah runs in the course of these verses, which are followed by mention of the obstinacy of the polytheists of Arabia, so that whoever is granted success may take heed through them: ﴿That We may make it for you a reminder, and that an attentive ear may retain it.﴾

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 69, verse 4:

When he had mentioned the condition of those among the earlier nations who were destroyed, because of the evil of their denial and the ugliness of their obstinacy, he followed that with mention of the threat of the Hereafter: ﴿On that Day you will be exposed; not a secret of yours will remain hidden﴾ [al-Haqqah: 18]. Then the discourse returned to what the surah of ﴿Nun. By the pen﴾ [al-Qalam: 1] was built upon: [affirming] his purity and honour (ﷺ), swearing to that: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble Messenger. And it is not the word of a poet; little do you believe. Nor is it the word of a soothsayer; little do you remember﴾ [al-Haqqah: 40-42]. It ended with the negation of what they had fabricated against him, he being specifically described as free of every flaw of that kind in the two surahs: ﴿You are not, by the favour of your Lord, a madman﴾ [al-Qalam: 2]. ﴿And what you have brought is not the word of a poet, nor the word of a soothsayer. Rather, it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds. And indeed, it is a reminder to the righteous. And indeed, We know that among you are deniers. And indeed, it is a certainty of truth﴾ [al-Haqqah: 41-51]. ﴿So exalt the name of your Lord, the Great﴾ [al-Haqqah: 52], [glorifying Him] above the great [falsehood] that they committed. [End.]

When the frightening had reached its limit, and the cause of denying the Hour was the belief that there was no power over it at all, or [the belief in] lack of knowledge of particulars, [He said, indicating complete power and knowledge over universals and particulars], warning whoever denied it that He is able to hasten the retribution, but out of His honouring of this Community He delayed its punishment until the Hereafter, except for those among them who are of the elite, for He will make them manifest in this world so as to complete their bliss after death. He began with the tribes most intense in denying the Resurrection, because their she-camel was the first sign of the power over it. And despite that they said: ﴿Shall we follow a single human being from among us?﴾ [al-Qamar: 24], until they said: ﴿Rather, he is a liar, an insolent one﴾ [al-Qamar: 25]. And in denying it [they said]: ﴿Does he promise you that when you have died and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 35]. ﴿Far, far is what you are promised﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 36]. ﴿There is only our worldly life; we die and we live﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 37], and so on. The matter concerning them revolves between 'Ad and Thamud: ﴿Thamud denied﴾ [al-Haqqah: 5]. Their being mentioned first is also because their land is nearer to Quraysh, and the admonition of nearness is greater. Their destruction was by the Blast (al-Sayhah), which is more like the blast of the Trumpet in the Horn, [by which] what is in the graves will be scattered. ﴿And 'Ad﴾ [al-Haqqah: 6]. The original construction would have been: "by it," but He made it manifest by describing it with what increases its greatness and terror, so He said: ﴿by the Striking Calamity﴾ [al-Haqqah: 4], i.e., that which strikes, that is, is struck with a strong blow, and pounds with a violent, severe pounding, [a pounding] upon the ears and the whole world, with the splitting of the heavens, the scattering of the stars, and the crumbling of the firm mountains. So nothing will stand firm against that terror.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 69, verse 5:

When He had grouped them together in denial, He separated them in punishment, on account of that denial, saying: ﴿As for Thamud﴾, and they are the people of Salih (peace be upon him).

Since what terrified them, owing to their being bound to sensible things, was only the punishment, and not who inflicted it, He framed the words ﴿they were destroyed﴾ in the passive voice, meaning: by the least of Our commands ﴿by the Overwhelming Blast﴾, that is, the Cry (al-sayha) which exceeded its limit in severity, so that the earth and the hearts quaked from it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 69, verse 6:

When he had mentioned those who were destroyed by the Blast [ṣayḥah] because they denied the Striking Calamity [al-qāriʿah], as a warning to whoever denies it, he followed it with those who were destroyed [ – al-muhlikīn –] by that which is the cause of the Blast's execution and its intensification, as evidence of the complete power over every kind of punishment by choice (p-343). Thus Exalted is He said: ﴿And as for ʿAd﴾, and they are the people of Hud, peace be upon him, ﴿they were destroyed﴾ [al-Haqqah: 5], that is, in the most severe manner for them and the easiest for what is within Our power, ﴿by a violent wind﴾, that is, it was at the extreme of intense cold and sound, as if it repeated the cold until it [ burns with its intensity and the sound until it ] deafens with its force. Al-Malawi said: its root is ṣarra, which means intense cold or intense heat. ﴿Insolent﴾, that is, exceeding the limit because of the intensity of its blast and the magnitude of its crash, acting like the arrogant one who cares for nothing, so its keepers could not control it, and those punished by it could not turn it back or restrain it. Rather, it would tear them from their hiding places that they had dug out and their fortresses that they had perfected and chosen, and destroy them. Al-Malawi said: ʿAli ibn Abi Talib and Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "No water or wind has ever descended except by a measure, through the hand of an angel, except on the day of the Flood, when Allah the Exalted permitted the water and it overpowered its keepers, and on the day of ʿAd, when He permitted the wind and it became insolent against its keepers." End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 69, verse 7:

When He described it (the wind) as being excessively violent against the creation and overpowering them, to a degree that made it a breach of habit, the like of which had not come before or after, He indicated its insignificance in relation to His greatness, and that it was He who brought it into being, not nature or anything else. Rather, it existed only by His power and His choice, as a subjugation of those who challenged His dominion and denied His messengers in what they reported about the Hour (al-sa'ah), which is the locus of wisdom and the manifestation of all His greatness. So He said, beginning a new statement to indicate this: ﴿He subjected it﴾, that is, He overpowered it so that He gave it dominion. Taskhir (subjugation) means using a thing with power. He indicated that this subjugation was one of punishment, not mercy or correction, by the particle of elevation (isti'la'), so He said: ﴿upon them﴾. He imposed this on it and made it pliant to Him, so that, despite its violence, it could only be obedient to His command and a product of His greatness and dominance.

Since this surah is for establishing matters, uncovering what is obscure, and clarifying what is hidden, it established the time of their punishment with a precision not previously matched. So He mentioned the days and the nights, and He placed the nights first, because calamities in them are more dreadful, more hideous, and more shameful, due to the scarcity of help, ignorance of the means of escape, and concealment of the aims and outlets. Also, because the number (of these periods) is masculine in form, and the masculine form of a word indicates the strength of its meaning more clearly. For this reason He made the specified noun a plural of abundance (jam' kathrah). Also, because they are seven, and seven is an emphatic number and the most comprehensive of numbers, as will be verified shortly in the context of the bearers of the Throne. It is not possible to suppose, from the placement of the nights first, that the beginning of the punishment was in them, because that would require the number of days to match, and so He said: ﴿seven nights﴾, meaning the wind did not let up in them for an instant, because its violence was intensified to a degree never matched before and never to be repeated after. ﴿And eight days﴾, likewise, while it was ﴿barren﴾ (husum), plural of hasim, meaning with a force that prevents any action, constant and continuous with no pause, from hasm al-kayy (cauterization), when one applies the branding iron repeatedly. It was cutting off every good and uprooting it. So it swept over them without any pause at all throughout the whole time, annihilating them so that not one of them remained. It is said that an old woman among them hid in a crevice, and it tore her out and destroyed her. For this reason these days were named "the days of the old woman." Or it was named so because they were the "old age" (ajuz) of winter, characterized by cold and violent winds. They ran from the morning of Wednesday, eight nights remaining of Shawwal, to the setting of the following Wednesday, which was the last of the month. It follows from the increase in the number of days that the beginning was definitely with them, otherwise the nights would not have been seven. So reflect upon this.

Since the barren (hasim) is the destroyer, He stated a consequence of it, depicting their past condition: ﴿So you see the people﴾, that is, those who were at the height of power over what they attempted, ﴿in it﴾, that is, in that period of days and nights, none of them was spared, ﴿felled﴾, that is, flung down upon the ground, dead, crushed, the wind having overwhelmed each of them with its intense pressure, humiliation and abasement evident upon them. (Sari' is the plural of sarie.) ﴿As if they were trunks of﴾, that is, roots of, ﴿palm trees﴾ that have grown old and decrepit, being in the utmost state of weakness and senility, ﴿hollow﴾, that is, with their insides eaten away, fallen. (Khawa is from khawā al-najm, when a star sets, and from khawā al-manzil, when it is emptied of its inhabitants.) It is said: the wind would enter through their mouths and expel what was inside their bodies through their backsides. So the description with this is due to the enormity of their bodies, the wind cutting them to pieces, severing their heads, their being devoid of life, and the blackening of them.

Since this was a matter awe-inspiring to anyone with even minimal understanding, and since interrogation is something that increases the awe, He said, giving the reason for their annihilation, so that the report of it, which entails the utmost knowledge of particulars, would be like a claim accompanied by its proof: ﴿So do you see﴾, i.e., O addressee who is informed, any of the people in all the regions ﴿remaining of them﴾, i.e., specifically, and he intensified the negation and expressed it with the verbal noun attached to the (feminine) ta' marbuta for emphasis, so he said: ﴿any remnant﴾, i.e., any survival, or a soul described as surviving. Allah, glorified and exalted be He, saved Salih (peace be upon him) and those who believed with him [from among Thamud], and the tyranny did not harm them. And Hud (peace be upon him) and those who believed with him from among 'Ad, none of them perished. This clearly indicates that He, exalted is He, has perfect knowledge of particulars, just as He has complete encompassing of universals, and indicates His power, His choice, and His wisdom. Thus the Muslim is not to be treated as equal to the criminal, nor the evildoer as equal to the doer of good.

When God had informed about those He destroyed by the wind, and about those whom the wind destroyed through a close cause without any intermediary, and since all of that was beyond the normal course of events, it refuted the people of nature (ahl al-tabā'i', the naturalists). He then informed about those whom the wind destroyed through an intermediary, namely the clouds, which brought the water. This was the cause of their being overtaken, even though their disbelief was in ta'til (the denial of the Creator's attributes), which is the most wretched kind of disbelief, because of the doctrine of nature (al-tabī'a), which entails denying the resurrection. Their drowning was by something that contradicted their belief, since it was beyond the normal course of events. So He said, drawing attention to the strength of their disbelief in the coming: ﴿And Pharaoh came﴾, that is, he came with a lofty and mighty coming. ﴿Pharaoh﴾, that is, the one whom We had made king over a part of the earth, who transgressed, acted tyrannically, and claimed divinity, forgetting Our awe and Our power through Our vengeance, denied the Maker, and spoke of nature. ﴿And those before him﴾, that is, in his direction, in his realm, and in what followed him, and in following his conduct, of exalting themselves in the earth without right and of arrogance in disbelief. This is a locative adverb (ẓarf makān). On the reading of the Basrans and al-Kisa'i, with a kasra on the kaf and a fatha on the bā' (i.e., ﴿qablahu﴾ with the bā' vowelled), it encompasses every disbelieving, arrogant person before him and after him. This is the meaning of the reading of the others, with a fatha on the qāf and sukūn on the bā', taken as an adverb of time corresponding to "ba'd" (after) with the addition of a meaning.

Since the people of Lut, peace be upon him, had gathered kinds of wickedness in which no one else had joined them, their punishment included what no punishment had been like. Each of their deeds, which no one among the worlds had preceded them in, and their punishment, the like of which had not existed before or after, refuted the people of nature. He singled them out from among those who were included in "those before him," on both readings, and said: ﴿And the overturned cities﴾, that is, the people of the towns that were overturned with their inhabitants, until the upper part became the lower, since what befell their people was an overturning, until they became that. Stones of brimstone followed them, the earth swallowed them, and they were covered by what has no like in the earth. These were the villages of the people of Lut, peace be upon him. ﴿With the sin﴾, that is, with error, or with deeds involving error that led on from them to the very vile act itself, such as sodomy, slapping, and breaking wind, together with polytheism and other kinds of wickedness, obstinacy, and transgression.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 69, verse 10:

Since all the messengers were together like a single individual, because their aims in calling to Allah and urging obedience to Him were in agreement, He said, beginning a new statement, causing this to follow from their coming with it, using a singular form in the wording for what suits the many by intending the genus: ﴿But they disobeyed﴾, i.e., they opposed and rejected, ﴿the messenger of their Lord﴾, i.e., every nation opposed the one whom its Benefactor had sent to it, the One who originated them from nothingness, deposited faculties in them, provided for them, and sent their messenger to guide them, deceived by His beneficence. They did not allow that the Benefactor could have power to harm as He has power to benefit, since He is the Harmer just as He is the Benefactor. So, to draw attention to the like of this, it is not permissible to transfer one of the two names from the other. He made the disobedience the cause of His saying: ﴿So He seized them﴾, i.e., their Lord seized them with a seizing of subjugation and wrath, ﴿a seizing﴾ that left none of them of any nation who had denied the Messenger. It was not like one who gives victory over an enemy from among the sons of Adam, who must inevitably let many of them escape him however hard he strives in the pursuit. This was only for the completeness of His knowledge, glorified and exalted is He, of particulars and universals, and the comprehensiveness of His power. And that seizing, together with its being of this magnitude in that it seized them as one soul, He, glorified is He, made ﴿overwhelming﴾, i.e., high above them, lofty in rank, in the strength of its assault and the severity of its destruction, exceeding the limit and growing in proportion to the increase of their deeds in ugliness. And "rabaa" means growth, and its root meaning is increase. So He drowned Pharaoh and his hosts, and drowned everyone who denied Noah, peace be upon him, and they were all the people of the earth other than those who boarded the ark with him. And He carried the cities of Lot, peace be upon him, after uprooting them from the earth, upon the back of the wind, by means of angels commanded by Him to do so, then He overturned them, sent stones after them, caused them to sink into the earth, and submerged them with foul water, the like of which is not found on earth.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 69, verse 11:

When it may have occurred to someone to wonder at the existence of Pharaoh and those after him, given the report of the destruction of those before him according to the reading of the majority, even though "min" (مِن, "from/any") is a word of generality, he pointed out that [He destroyed] all those who opposed and saved all those who agreed. As an answer to that question, he said, emphasizing it for the sake of the one who seeks to make difficulties, and because this was among the things one marvels at and takes delight in mentioning: ﴿Indeed We﴾, that is, (p-350) by Our power, Our greatness, and Our encompassing [knowledge], ﴿when the water overflowed﴾, that is, it increased beyond its limit until it rose above the highest mountain on earth, to the extent that whoever was upon it drowned, when the people of Noah, upon him be peace, drowned us [by it]. They could not control it, nor did they confront it in any way, nor were they guided to board the ship; so its going beyond the customary course was a refutation of the people of natural causes.

Since bringing into existence is a blessing, and saving their forefathers from drowning was such that it became the cause of their existence, [this] became a retribution upon them, the Exalted said: ﴿We carried you﴾, that is, in the loins of your forefathers, by Our majesty, Our will, and Our power, ﴿in the sailing vessel﴾, that is, the ship which We made, by Our wisdom, firmly adept at sailing, as if there were no other sailing vessel upon the surface of the water which We made to be of a nature to drown, and this is an expression of the attribute in place of the thing described. Noah, upon him be peace, was the first to build a ship, and he built it only by the revelation of God Most High and by His protection of him from slipping in its construction. He said: make it in the shape of the breast of a bird, so that what moves in the water would be close to what moves in the air. And He drowned all of the people of the earth other than those in the ship, of humans and others.

(p-٣٥١) When He, glory be to Him and exalted, began with Thamud, who were the nearest of the destroyed peoples to the honored Mecca, because warning by what is nearest is more effective, and concluded with the people of Noah, peace be upon him, because they were the entire population of the earth, and their affair was not feared to be repeated by anyone after them, He gave the reason for choosing their deliverance by the ship rather than by anything else, saying: ﴿That We may make it﴾, meaning these great acts: the deliverance of the believers so that none of them perished by that punishment, and the destruction of the disbelievers so that none of them escaped. Likewise, the ship in which We carried Noah, peace be upon him, and those with him, by preserving it, is one of His signs, a marvel among His wondrous proofs, and a rare wonder of its kind through the ages. ﴿For you﴾, meaning O humankind, ﴿a reminder﴾, meaning a great means for recalling the first act of its origination and for admonition through it, so that you may infer from it the perfection of His power, exalted be He, the completeness of His knowledge, and the greatness of His mercy and His dominion. That will lead you to Him, and you will turn your hearts toward Him. ﴿And retain it﴾, meaning that the story of the ship and other things mentioned before may be preserved, preserved firmly and steadily, as if it were contained in a vessel.

(p-٣٥٢) Since the one who benefits from what he hears and retains it is very few, He indicated this by using the singular for the ear, and He said, in the singular and indefinite form while indicating its great value: ﴿An attentive ear﴾, meaning one of great benefit. ﴿Attentive﴾, meaning it is of its nature to retain what ought to be retained of the divine words and deeds and the lordly secrets, for the benefit of God's servants, as Noah, peace be upon him, and those with him did, though they were few, as a cause for the continuation of offspring and blessing in them, until the earth was filled with them. ("Wa'y" is retention in the mind, and "iya'" is retention in a vessel.) In this there is a rebuke of people for the scarcity of those among them who are attentive, and an indication that a single ear which is heedless of God, exalted be He, is the majority, while whatever else there is, God does not regard them at all. This was said by al-Asfahani, al-Zamakhshari, and others.

When He mentioned the Resurrection and the terror of its matter by means of the expression *al-Ḥāqqah* and others, and indicated His power over it and His wisdom through the stories of those He mentioned [ عَلى -] in the manner that has passed, until He concluded with those whose story most resembled those stories in relation to the Resurrection, in that God's command in it encompassed the people of the earth within a short time, and those who were saved from it, compared to those who were destroyed, were like a white hair on the hide of a black bull, He made the statement "So when the Trumpet is blown" a consequence of all that has passed, as an explanation of its matter. He put the verb in the passive form to indicate how easy that is for Him, and that what is produced by Him does not depend on a specific blower. Rather, whoever He appoints from His soldiers for that purpose, what He wills is produced by him and mentioned. The verb's subject is feminine, [ التَّأْنِيثِ -] because it is separated from the verb, and because its femininity is not real, and to indicate the [ قُوَّةِ -] force of the blowing. "In the Trumpet" means the horn into which Isrāfīl (peace be upon him) blows. It is as if He expressed it with it rather than with "the horn" for example, because by it there is sometimes the annihilation of forms and sometimes their creation and their return to their shapes. Its mouth is as wide as the distance between the heavens and the earth. (p-٣٥٣) He attributed the verb to the verbal noun (*maṣdar*) so that it would convey the blowing at its very beginning, not to emphasize it, although emphasis is understood from it, and it is not intended in itself. So He said: "a single blast." Since the verb indicated the single occurrence, He emphasized it, to show His great power and the insignificance of things before Him, by saying: "one." That is, all creation perishes. Thus they said that this blast is the first one, and at it the world is ruined. The apparent context, however, is that it is the second, by which resurrection occurs. The ruin of what was mentioned after their rising is more fitting, because it is more awe-inspiring for them. That it is the second is one of the two reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both.

When he mentioned the effect (of Allah's power) in giving life, he followed it with the effect on inanimate things. He began with the lower things, because of their closeness to man, so that the lesson he draws from them is greater. He said: ﴿And the earth is carried [i.e. -] the spread-out one and shaken with a violent shaking, and the mountains [i.e. -] in which lies their stability, so they were lifted from their places, and were crumbled to powder, and became scattered dust, with no stone or kudya (a hard, compact lump of earth or rock) left in them.

When the force of the crushing and the completeness of its effect was intended, he made the mountains one thing and said: ﴿So they are crushed﴾, i.e., the two masses (the earth and the mountains) leveled the earth and its stakes (the mountains), were spread out, and some of them were ground against others, ﴿with one crushing﴾, i.e., they became a heap of loose sand, and were made level with the greatest ease, so that nothing of one could be distinguished from the other, but they became in the utmost evenness. From their saying: ناقَةٌ دَكّاءُ (naqatun dakkā'), i.e., a she-camel with no hump; and أرْضٌ دَكّاءُ (ardun dakkā'), i.e., a land that is wide and level. (p-354) They said: al-dakk (crushing) and al-daqq (grinding) are brothers, and al-dakk is more emphatic. Abu Hayyan said: in al-dakk there is the separation of the parts, and in al-daqq there is the mixing of the parts.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 69, verse 15:

When he mentioned the blowing of the Trumpet, he made His saying ﴿So on that Day﴾ a consequence of it, meaning: when they are crushed. It is a *badal* (substitute, in grammatical terms) for ﴿idhā﴾ ("when"). He repeated it because of the long separation between them, and it conveys its dread and magnification. He put the *zarf* (adverbial complement of time) in the governance of His saying ﴿the Inevitable Event has occurred﴾, meaning: the event by which the promise and the threat were made. So it was as if it were a thing extremely heavy, with nothing to hold it up. Thus, of itself, it has nothing but to fall. It is the Resurrection (al-Qiyamah), the Inevitable (al-Haqqah), and the Striking Calamity (al-Qari'ah). He varied its names to convey its dread, meaning: the Resurrection has come to pass. The intended meaning of it is the second blast.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 69, verse 16:

When he had mentioned the effect of the lower world, he mentioned the upper world, saying: ﴿And the sky will be split open﴾, meaning this kind (of thing) because of the severity of that Day. [And since a thing is not split except due to a defect in it, he made his saying following it a confirmation of that:] ﴿So it, on that Day﴾, meaning when the Inevitable Event occurs, ﴿will be frail﴾, meaning weak, falling apart, light, not holding together.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 69, verse 17:

Since it is the custom, as is known, that a king displays various aspects of his majesty on the day of reviewing the troops, He said, informing us in a manner similar to what we are accustomed to: ﴿And the angels﴾ — meaning this category, which applies to one and to more than one, whereas the plural does not apply to what is less than a plurality; so this is more comprehensive. ﴿will be upon its sides﴾ — meaning the regions of the sky, its edges and its borders, of that which has not split apart. Ad-Dahhak said: "They will be there until Allah commands them, and they will descend and encompass the earth and whoever is upon it." [End of quotation.]

It has also been said: the "sides" (arja') of the earth, whose singular is raja (a shortened form), and the dual is rajawan. So they will encompass jinn and mankind and gather them like the gathering of game for the purpose of seizing it.

Since the king displays on the day of reviewing his throne of sovereignty and the seat of his might, He said: ﴿And will bear the throne﴾ of ﴿your Lord﴾ — meaning the One who does good to you in everything He wills, especially on that day, through what appears of your elevation. Since this is an awe-inspiring matter that rends hearts, He mentioned this, giving comfort to the one to whom it was revealed and assuring him against everything he fears.

Since the throne is general to the whole direction of above, He omitted the preposition and said: ﴿above them﴾ — meaning above their heads ﴿on that day﴾, meaning the day when the Inevitable Event occurs, ﴿eight﴾ in number, according to the number of what lies beneath it, namely the seven heavens and the Kursi. ﴿Eight﴾ — meaning of the angels, individuals or ranks, whose bearers, the four in this world, are strengthened by four others, because of the severity of that day [and its weight]. This is in a hadith transmitted by Abu Dawud, at-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Abu Ya'la and al-Baghawi from al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib (may Allah be pleased with him), and its outward meaning is that they are individuals. Its wording is: "Eight wild goats, between their knees and hooves is as the distance between the heaven and the earth." The outward meaning of this is that they are in this world. That they are four only in this world has been mentioned by the commentators, and at-Tabarani transmitted it through the chain of Ibn Ishaq, who said: "It has reached us that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

'They are four today, and when the Day of Resurrection comes, He will strengthen them with four others.'" It is also mentioned in the lengthy hadith of the Trumpet, which Abu Ya'la and others narrate through Isma'il ibn Rafi', from Yazid ibn Ziyad, from al-Qurtubi, from a man, from Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him). This number may be intended to refer to the people of the seven heavens and the Kursi, which makes eight, and they are a creation none can count but Allah, glorified and exalted be He, and this better suits the manifestation of majesty. [It is also possible that by them is meant eight individuals, and their bearing it would be more manifest in majesty —] so that everyone who sees this may know that their likes cannot bear the like of it in its greatness and encompassing. This is the most evident of the meanings in the hadiths related concerning it. The choice of this number is more fitting to the aspect preceding it, because it exceeds the number set for emphasis, which is seven, [by one], indicating that it is more emphatic than the number of emphasis, since it points to the fact that whenever you intensify, the matter exceeds your intensification by that which is the first of the numbers. This indicates the absence of ending and of stopping at a limit. To this also points (p-357) that the eighth has the fractions a half, a quarter and an eighth, which are seven in total, and seven is a number comprehensive of all types of number: odd, even, even of even and even of odd. All of this indicates exaggeration in [displaying] majesty, grandeur and might, and it is an illustration for us by means of what we know of the states of kings. Otherwise:

"The matter is greater than the saying of any speaker..."

"Whether eloquent men make it delicate or make it grand."

It is to make known the greatness of that day, so that the servants may fear and adhere to the causes of felicity. What I have said concerning the secret of seven has been mentioned by Imam Badr al-Din ibn al-Damamini, companion of our shaykhs, in the discussion of the waw in his marginal notes on Ibn Hisham's Mughni, citing the tafsir of 'Imad al-Kindi, judge of Alexandria, entitled al-Kafil bi-ma'ani al-Tanzil. He said: Ustadh 'Abd Allah al-Kafif al-Maliqi related that it is an eloquent dialect of some Arabs to say: "wahid, ithnan, thalatha, arba'a, khamsa, sitta, sab'a, thamaniya, tis'a, 'ashara" — this is their dialect — and whenever the word thamaniya appears in their speech, they insert the waw. Some of our companions have composed verses on the seven being the final limit of number, which are:

"O you who ask about the secret of the number's being limited to seven and not exceeding it,
Nothing has gladdened it except the confinement of its divisions
In one odd and a supported thing,
And that thing which you support is confined in one and more..."

"So the odd and the odd, when they are joined, make a pair with the odd which is not supported;
Two and two, when they are joined, make four, which gathers with the shade of the hand;
Then that is seven when completed: four and two with a single one;
And what comes after this is a repetition of it, not an additional increase in number.
Three with its like makes six, which has passed, and what has passed is not counted;
And thus four with its like is a pair and a pair that has passed; do not add."

Imam Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Karim al-Shahrastani said in the introduction to his book al-Milal wa'l-Nihal: Most of the people of number hold that one is not included in number. The origin of number is the first two, and it divides into even and odd. The first odd is three and the first even is four. What lies beyond four is a repetition, like five, which is composed of an odd and an even, and it is called the circular number. Six is composed of two odds, and it is called the perfect number. Seven is composed of an odd and an even, and it is called the complete number. Eight is composed of two evens, and it is the beginning of the other series. So calculation proceeds in correspondence with one, which is the cause of number and is not included in it; therefore it is odd, having no brother.

Since number originates from two, the fundamental is confined to two divisions. (p-359) Since number divides into odd and even, its origin is confined to seven: the first odd is three and the first even is four, which is the limit; and what is other than them is composed of them. The simple elements of number in general are one, two, three and four, which are perfection; whatever exceeds them of composite numbers are all composites, without limit. Abu al-Hakam ibn Burjan said in his tafsir of Surat al-Qadr: The limit of number is six, and the seventh is its odd.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 69, verse 18:

Having reached the utmost point in warning the servants about the Day of Mutual Callingout (al-tanad), and since they have two states, the particular and the general, the general being the presentation (al-'ard) and the particular being the division into one who does good and one who does evil, he increased its magnitude by saying: ﴿On that day﴾, that is, if what has preceded is the case.

Since what is terrifying is the presentation itself, he made its verb passive, and also because it is the speech of those who have power, and so he said: ﴿you will be presented﴾, that is, before Allah, glorified and exalted, for reckoning, just as a sultan presents the army in order to examine their affairs, so that he may choose from among them the one who is fit for honour, closeness and reward, and the one who is corrupt for distancing, punishment and affliction. He expressed the reckoning by the presentation, which is a part of it. The one who does good will have nothing but that, while the one who does evil will be called to account. ﴿Not one of you will be hidden﴾, that is, on that day, from anyone in any way whatsoever. ﴿Not one of you will be hidden﴾, that is, on that day, from anyone [in any way] whatsoever, ﴿concealed﴾, that is, nothing of concealment will occur at all [in any] of the states regarding a thing which in this world was meant to be hidden, neither of deeds nor of souls, even if it is in the utmost subtlety and obscurity, because that day is the day of complete manifestation from the graves and from the breasts, and other matters, so that this may be more glorious for the happiness of the one who is happy, and more shameful for the wretchedness of the one who is wretched, and so he is far removed. Abu Musa, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "There are three presentations. As for the first two, they involve disputation and excuses. As for the third, at that point the scrolls will fly open," so he took [his book] in his right hand and took [his book] in his left.

Since it is known that they are of two kinds, a doer of good and a doer of evil, and the implied sense is: We shall give each one of you the record of his deeds, comprising his actions, his sayings, and all his dispositions and states. Among you is one to whom it is handed in his right hand, so his good deeds are made manifest to him and his evil deeds are concealed from him. Among you is one who is given it in his left hand, so his evil deeds are made manifest to him and his good deeds are erased, because he was given his reward in this world through the good things that were hastened for him. He then joined to this, as a detailed explanation, His saying: ﴿As for him who is given his record﴾. He put the verb in the passive form because the sign of happiness is the act of falling into the right hand, not from a specific giver. ﴿His record﴾, that is, the one in which his deeds were recorded. ﴿In his right hand, he will say﴾, because of what he sees of his happiness, exulting in his state and displaying the blessing of his Lord, since a person is naturally inclined to display the good that has been bestowed upon him, completing his pleasure by subduing his enemies and gladdening his friends. It is said that his evil deeds are written in the inner part of his record and his good deeds in its outer part, so he reads the inner part while people read the outer part. When he finishes, it is said to him: "Allah has forgiven them; turn the page." Then His saying ﴿Here, read﴾ means: take, you who are present among the creatures, the angels and others. In it there is a sound understood to mean "take" (p-361). It is connected sometimes with a kaf and sometimes with a hamza, and it is an ism fi'l (a verbal noun functioning as a verb). He chose it here to show that its address is to all the people of the standing place, whether they are hidden among them (angels, jinn and others) or apparent. This is because the alif, according to the rabbaniyyun (the spiritually knowing ones), is unseen and encompassing, as its point of articulation indicates. For them it is therefore an expression of the Supreme Standing, the All-Encompassing. This meaning is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. The hamza is the beginning of His unseen, and for this reason its point of articulation is the furthest of the guttural letters, indicating this. The beginning of the unseen of Allah, glory be to Him, is His acts, which include the apparent and the hidden. Its origin is the kaf. For them it is a complete manifestation possessing independence, which is the one whose nature is to be manifest, and the offspring of the kind are more worthy of this. This is indicated by the point of articulation of the kaf, which comes after the qaf, from the root of the tongue nearest its middle. The object of "ma" is elided according to the Basrah grammarians, and it is indicated by "kitabiyah" in His saying ﴿Read my record﴾. Its hā' is for pausing, as if it were an indication of the severity of distress on that day, showing that if this fortunate one needs a pause after every clause for rest and cannot proceed in speech, then what of others? It also indicates, along with that, the completion of the matter, the finality of the judgment, and the certainty that it will not be changed.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 69, verse 20:

Since the reality of the reckoning (*ḥisāb*) is the recounting of deeds and the requital for them, and since the human being, because he is inclined toward deficiency, cannot measure God by His true measure, and the higher a person is, the greater his awareness of his own deficiency, and whoever is called to account in detail (*nūqisha al-ḥisāb*), as the Prophet ﷺ said, is punished, he said, emphasizing, because the one who sees his state and his book denies that he has any sin or any shortcoming: ﴿Indeed, I thought﴾, meaning on this day, out of fear of the evil of my deeds, which I know about myself, ﴿that I would meet﴾, meaning that it would be firmly established for me, a firmness that never ceases, that I would encounter ﴿my reckoning﴾ before the Judge (*al-Dayyān*). This is because I was one who combined, as I was commanded, between fear and hope. I feared that He would set my good deeds against the blessings, and no smallest blessing would stand for me, so I would be punished for my evil deeds, and I hoped for His forgiveness. So He, glory be to Him, fulfilled my hope and granted security from my fear. Thus I now know that I am not called to account in detail, and that my reckoning is only the presentation (*al-ʿarḍ*), which is the easy reckoning, by which my deeds are presented so that I am not requited for their evil and am rewarded for their good, out of grace, mercy, bounty, and blessing. It is also possible that the *ẓann* (thought) refers to the worldly life, and that it is used to mean certainty (*yaqīn*), indicating that for the intelligent person, the thought of danger suffices as the fear that moves him to action. In this there is an indication of humbling the self, because a human being is never free of passing thoughts of doubt that occur to him and assail him, and an announcement that such things do not undermine firm belief, and an alert that the thought (*ẓann*) suffices in making action obligatory. Then it becomes, in that case, a reason for the giving of the book in the right hand. In it there is also a rebuke to the disbelievers and a declaration against them that they did not reach, in this certain matter, even the level of thought, so how about the certainty of knowledge? Yet they neglected to act upon it, and so they opposed it.

Since the assessment of this was clear, he caused, by the consequence of the easy reckoning, the bestowal of reward, so He said: ﴿So he will be in a pleasant life﴾, meaning a state of life.

Since contentment with a thing does not occur except when it reaches the utmost of what is desired and the ultimate of what is hoped for, He said, attributing the contentment to the life metaphorically (kināyah) for the contentment of its possessor in the most eloquent manner: ﴿well-pleasing﴾, meaning that contentment is established for him and constant for it, because it is at the height of goodness and perfection. The Arabs do not express most kinds of happiness by anything more than "a pleasing life," in the sense that its people are content with it. The criterion for the perfection of pleasure is contentment [or -] that, were the life to have intellect, it would be content with its own state.

Since Allah, glory be to Him, had aroused longing for the state of the one who possesses this pleasant life, and since it had been stated in summary, He detailed and clarified it by substituting for it, adding to the stirring of desire, so He said: ﴿In a lofty garden﴾, that is, gardens comprising everything that is desired from them.

And since the nobility of a dwelling lies in its height, He said: ﴿lofty﴾, that is, in place, in rank, in buildings, in levels, in trees, and in every respect.

Because it is in the nature of lofty things that they are hard to reach, He said: ﴿Its clusters are near﴾, i.e., "clusters" is the plural of qift (قِطف, with a kasra), which is what is picked from the fruits gathered together on one of its stalks; "near" means easy to pick and extremely easy to reach, for the rider, the one standing, the one sitting, and the one lying down, all of it equally, always, without interruption or hardship for any of its people in taking any of that.

(p. 365) Since the fruits being in this state indicates abundant irrigation, and abundant irrigation indicates the source of drink, and since they [the fruits] are among the singular words that carry a general meaning, He used singular pronouns for their wording, specifying each individual one, while using plural forms for their meaning, to inform that all of its people share in the blessings whether alone or together. So He said: ﴿Eat and drink﴾ [meaning:] it is theirs, that is, it is permitted for them. This indicates that there is no prohibition on it, and that they are commanded to it explicitly, as evidence of the pleasure of the Lord of the Garden, so that their life is not spoiled for them by any kind of thing that might be feared as harmful. The object is omitted to signal generality, lest one suppose that some part of it is excluded, and so it becomes a cause of temptation, as happened to Adam, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him.

Since food and drink in this abode produce indigestion and illness, and in it there is what is not pleasant, and since what happened to our father Adam and our mother Eve, upon them be peace and blessings, from eating a single morsel, was known for its bad outcome, [God] said, giving them good news about that: ﴿Wholesome﴾, that is, eating that is good, delicious, and pleasant, together with distance from every harm and safety of outcome in every respect. There is no waste there of urine, excrement, spittle, mucus, filth, dirt, weakness, headache, heaviness, or anything harmful.

Since He stimulated their desire for the effects, He led them to their causes and urged them to compete in attaining them and to persevere in increasing them. So He said, adding to their pleasure, that this is by way of recompense, and that no one among the creatures has any favour over them in any of it. For the thing most beloved to a person is to eat from what his right hand has gained and what he has acquired by his own work, together with the honour that this carries: ﴿for what you sent forward﴾, that is, what you gave of yourselves for your afterlife, willingly, of righteous deeds, and for what you left of the worldly life, which is lowly in comparison with what you were compensated for of the works of the heart, the body, and wealth. ﴿In the days﴾. Since He, glorified is He, had guaranteed everything a person occupies himself with of the interests of his worldly life, so that it reaches him without doubt even if he empties all his time for the worship of his Lord, He said: ﴿gone by﴾, that is, the days in the world that have passed and ended and whose toil you have rested from, and in which there was no distraction from worship, either by abandoning preoccupation with livelihood, for one who has attained the rank of reliance upon God, or by striving in moderation, intending to assist the servants in the affairs of this abode and to bestow favours upon them, and not to be a burden upon them without relying on one's own striving, but rather in obedience to the command, while being content with sufficiency.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 69, verse 25:

Since it is the custom that the people of the Gathering (al-'Ard) divide into two groups, accepted and rejected, and since He, glorified and exalted, mentioned the accepted first, to make the listener eager for their condition and to make him envy their outcome and good end, He followed it with the rejected, to make people averse to their deeds by mentioning the ugly aspects of their condition. So He said: ﴿But as for him who﴾. Since what indicates harm is the giving in an ugly manner, without specifying the giver, He spoke with the passive voice for this reason, and also to show the humiliation of being seized and his inability to refrain from anything that displeases him: ﴿is given his record in his left hand﴾, that is, the scroll of his deeds — may God protect us from that. ﴿So he will say﴾, that is, upon seeing the evil end that the veil has been lifted from for him, until he has no doubt about it, because of the ugly deeds he had sent ahead. Whatever comes that might suggest a pause on that day is from the category of arrogance and of defending falsehood in the manner he was in the world. ﴿Oh, I wish﴾ — an expression of wishing for the impossible. It flows, in continuity with what preceded, in the passive construction that indicates his humiliation and lack of natural capacity, so He said: ﴿I had not been given﴾, that is, from any giver, ﴿my record﴾, that is, this one which reminded me of the foulness of my deeds and informed me of their recompense.

﴿And I had not﴾, that is, and [O -] would that I had not ﴿known﴾, even if I had tried to gain knowledge of ﴿what﴾ [that is, -] the reality of ﴿my reckoning﴾, from the mention of the deed and the mention of its recompense. Rather, I persisted in being ignorant of that, just as I was in the world. (p-367)

Since he wished for these two things, he resumed stating his desire regarding them, saying: because he saw that what awaited him was worse than what he was in of the barzakh (the intermediate state). ﴿Would that it had been the end﴾, that is, the death through which he came, ﴿that had decided it all﴾, that is, the decisive, absolute, binding death that makes death permanent and is the final end of him, so that after it there would be no resurrection and nothing other than death, as I used to believe in the world. Imam al-Razi said: and in the hadith, "Wish for death" (tamannu al-mawt), that is, at that time, and there was nothing in the world more hateful to them than it.

When the wish was indicative, because it was the opposite of what he had wished for regarding the resurrection (al-ba'th), in accordance with what the messengers had informed him of, and regarding the reckoning (al-hisab), which is the secret and essence of the resurrection, and he had been saying that he would be saved from it by his wealth and his standing, if it were to happen, he said, giving the reason for his wish: ﴿What has my wealth availed me?﴾ This is a negation expressing regret over the loss of the benefit he had been hoping for. On this reading the object is omitted for generality. Or it is interrogative, an interrogation of denial directed at himself and of reproach, since his self had embellished for him what produced for him every evil and every impossibility, in opposition to the primordial nature (al-fitrah al-ula), which was confirmed by what the messengers had reported, until that embellishment brought him to ruin. ﴿Gone from me is my authority﴾, that is, the authority by which he withheld God's right and magnified himself over His servants. This negation of benefit is valid and understood under both readings, the declarative negation and the interrogative.

(p-368) Since wealth was the means of access to the sultan, he said, negating what his wealth had brought him and explaining why it did not avail him:

﴿My authority has perished from me.﴾ That is, it has passed away from me, so that it is as though I had not been in it even for a moment. "My authority" means my domination over those who call to God, by means of the false doubts which he would utter with his tongue, and I would support him in them despite their evident falsehood. The kingdom to which the wealth had brought him has perished, for that great dominion has perished, and the one who gives support is the most remote of the remote.

Since it is as if it were said: "This is what he said, so what is said [to them]?" I answer: it is said to the Zabaniyah (the angels of punishment), to torment his spirit through rebuke and through the command to punish him before the eyes of the witnesses: ﴿Seize him﴾, meaning, O Zabaniyah, those whom he used to belittle when he heard their mention.

Since seizing indicates humiliation arising from anger, its consequence is His saying: ﴿Then shackle him﴾, meaning, gather his hands to his neck and his feet from behind his nape to his forelock.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 69, verse 31:

Since the shackling (al-ghull) is followed by [further] punishment, he said, magnifying the rank of His punishment in severity and terror by expressing it with the particle of delay: ﴿Then the Blazing Fire (al-Jaheem)﴾, that is, the great Fire, which rears up against anyone who would try to repel it and recoils from those who see it, because it is at the extreme of heat, blazing, fury and harshness. ﴿Burn him (ṣallūhu)﴾, that is, make an intensive effort in roasting him in it (p-369), and repeat it, plunging him into the Fire again and again like a sheep being roasted, [and do] not roast him at first in anything other than it, because he used to spare no effort in burning the hearts of his advisers with the harshest speech and other means that he could muster, and he used to be arrogant towards the weak. So it was fitting that he be made to burn in the greatest of fires. He also expressed it with the particle of delay to indicate the high rank of what follows it, and so he said, signifying that there is no escape: ﴿Then in a chain﴾ [al-Haqqah: 32], that is, a chain extremely great, not one that is lesser than it.

When he put it first, it signified the importance given to it and its singling out because of the intensity of the dread it inspires. It was thus known through the magnitude of its terror and the severity of its horror, so that both the implicit meaning (mafhum) and the explicit meaning (manṭuq) would combine to express its awfulness. He said: ﴿its measure is seventy cubits﴾, that is, whatever measure it is assigned, in length or in breadth. ﴿Seventy cubits﴾ may be taken as a literal number, or it may be hyperbole. What indicates that it is hyperbole is what al-Tirmidhi narrated, and he said: its chain of transmission is ḥasan (fair; acceptable in rank), from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If a lump of lead like this one" — and he gestured towards something like a skull — "were sent down from the sky to the earth, a distance of five hundred years, it would reach the earth before nightfall. And if it were sent down from the top of the chain, it would travel for forty autumns, night and day, before it reached its base and its depth."

He, glorified is He, indicated its narrowness, relative to what surrounds the body, by expressing it with the word "threading" (salk), so He said: ﴿Then thread him﴾, that is, insert him in such a way that he is like the thread (silk), that is, the cord, which passes into the hole of a bead with difficulty because of the narrowness of that hole. This is either because it encircles his neck or his whole body, so that it winds around him, and he becomes in the utmost constriction and humiliation, unable to move at all. This is the punishment of the body, because he corrupted the heart by not believing, and the body by not doing deeds.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 69, verse 33:

When he had mentioned his punishment in general terms, he followed it with its causes, beginning with the greatest of them and emphasizing it, because every disbeliever, even the one who denies God's attributes (al-mu'attil), acknowledges God Most High in some form of acknowledgment and claims to have faith in Him in some form of claim, since he cannot do otherwise, owing to the overwhelming manifestness of Him, glory be to Him, and the spreading of His light and radiance: ﴿Indeed, he did not believe﴾ meaning, by disposition and nature, even if he displays something with which he deceives the weak and deludes the rich, ﴿in God﴾ meaning, the Supreme King who knows the secret and what is more hidden, ﴿now or in the future﴾ meaning, neither now nor in future time.

Since the greatness of the King necessitates an increase in punishment for whoever opposes Him in proportion to its loftiness, and since what brought this wretched one to this disgrace was his arrogance toward the command of God and His servants, he indicated that none deserves greatness other than Him, glory be to Him, and so said: ﴿the Mighty﴾, meaning, the one perfect in His greatness.

(p-371) When he had shown his enmity toward the Mighty King by corrupting the scholarly faculty [between what disbelief necessitates of contempt for the weak, a corruption of the practical faculty], to inform that he is charged with the branches of the Shari'ah just as he is charged with its roots, and to make clear that his enmity toward those above him stems from the baseness of his nature and not from the loftiness of his aspiration, He said, magnifying this sin by placing it in the context of disbelief, and by using the expression of urging (al-hadd), indicating thereby that the doer of this is intensely absorbed in love of the world, for nothing prevents him from urging others toward good except his hoarding for himself: ﴿And does not urge﴾, i.e., does not impel or incite, ﴿upon﴾ giving ﴿the food﴾ or feeding ﴿the poor﴾, i.e., facilitating it by helping in it if it exists, and asking for its giving and what stands in its place if it is absent; so how much more [would he not urge] giving from his own [wealth]? For that is not impelled except by faith, being free of any share [of the world]. The restriction is understood to mean that he urges the service of the great tyrants and loves to cling to their doorsteps. The idiom of "food" without "feeding" indicates that the poor possess their sufficiency from the wealth of the rich. This indicates that, together with his disbelief, he possesses the most vile of inward qualities: in extreme stinginess, hardness, and lack of manliness, by turning away from the causes of praise and from keeping oneself free of ill speech and ugly mention; and that is the most vile of vices. Therefore he specified these two matters.

Abu al-Darda', may Allah be pleased with him, used to urge the feeding of them and would say: "We have removed half of the chain by faith; shall we not remove the other?"

(p-372) That is, by urging feeding. And his censure for disdaining the poor implies censure for disdaining those beneath them who are in a worse condition, by way of a fortiori reasoning.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 69, verse 35:

When He, glory be to Him and exalted, had described him with the vilest beliefs and the most repugnant vices, He made the following statement a consequence of these, in contrast to the corruption of the two faculties of knowledge: ﴿So there is no friend for him today﴾. When He mentioned the time that follows the resurrection, He mentioned the place that exists in it, which is the Hereafter, [and so He said]: ﴿here﴾, that is, in the whole gathering of the Resurrection, ﴿a friend (ḥamīm)﴾, that is, a pure friend who is distressed on his behalf and protects him from the punishment, because they are all his enemies, just as he himself [used to be] not tender toward the weak in their poverty with regard to the fleeting goods of wealth.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 69, verse 36:

When He negated for him honor, due to his detachment from the party of the Sovereign, the Protecting, the Loving, and his inclining toward the party of Satan, the enemy, the ungrateful, He followed it with what is intended by wealth, from which arise all kinds of enjoyment, and which is sought for gatherings and companionship with friends, owing to his clinging to his wealth and his turning away from the dependents of the King, on account of their weakness, whom He had granted wealth and commanded to share it with them. So He said: ﴿Nor any food﴾. And since the exception is a criterion for generality, He said: ﴿except from ghislin﴾, that is, the washings of the people of the Fire from their scorching heat and their pus, two actions of washing. And it follows from this food that (p-373) it would be beneath something else, so that the water of its washing would flow to it.

Since he has restricted their food to something that no one would approach by choice, he now restricts those who consume it, describing them by the attribute that made it lawful for them to eat it. So he said: ﴿None eat it except the sinners﴾. The exception was left unfilled (al-istithna' al-mufarragh, the exception with its omitted antecedent) to draw attention to the fact that the excepted element is the intended point, as though there were no preceding term at all. So he said: ﴿except the sinners﴾. That is, only those who deliberately commit sins eat it, and no one else. The word derives from khati'a al-rajulu (with the pattern of fariḥa), spelled with a hamza, meaning a man who deliberately commits a sin. As for the mukhti' (one who errs), he is the one who intends good but fails to attain it without deliberate intent, as in ﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you have erred in﴾ [al-Ahzab: 5], that is, you intended what was right but did not hit it. This food cleanses what is in their bellies of the substances and qualities by which the one who holds them is sustained, and it is in the same position as the wealth they used to hoard, which they concealed within themselves and stored in their treasuries, keeping it to themselves at the expense of the weak.

When the Exalted One mentioned al-Haqqah (the Inevitable Reality), which He made the abode of reckoning for the doer of good and the doer of evil, whom His power divided and His wisdom required, and He directed the Qur'an, which is a reminder to the worlds, toward both of them through promise, warning, glad tidings and threat, and it is known by the immediate judgment of reason that it is not valid at all in anyone's wisdom to leave those under his authority neglected, especially if he has already commanded and forbidden them, and He established proof of His power over it by punishing those whom He uprooted because they denied His messengers, so that their punishment and the deliverance of the good-doers among them would be a [MATHAL-] tangible example in which the Inevitable Reality is witnessed, because whoever has power over that has complete power over every possibility, and He mentioned what wisdom indicates regarding the bestowing of blessings on the obedient and the punishment of the disobedient, through what is most fitting for the work of each of them, in these miraculous styles in terms of vocabulary, structures and meanings, this indicated [the matter at] the end of Surat "Nun," He returned to establishing it by another way, which is that, because of the completeness of His knowledge and the perfection of His power, He does not confirm the one who lies against Him in his lie, let alone support him. So, giving the reason for that when the matter reached its ultimate clarity, mentioning what is more emphatic than an oath, because some people of dialectical argument (jadal) when their opponent overcomes them say: "You only defeated me because you are more skilled than I am in argument, while the truth is with me," so his opponent swears to him that he did not deceive him and did not intend in his argument anything but the truth.

﴿So I swear by what you see﴾, meaning: an oath does not come from Me, ﴿by what﴾, meaning: by the totality of what ﴿you see﴾, meaning: for you there is the capacity to perceive it, of everything that has entered the world of witnessing.

(p-374)

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And what you do not see﴾.

That is, what is not within your capacity to see in this world, [namely] all existent things, the necessary and the contingent, the intelligible and the perceptible, because the matter is too clear to require an oath, although I swear in other places by whatever I will of the individual members of this totality.

(p-375) When he had emphasized the matter to the utmost degree by what he said, namely that [indeed] the matter had reached such clarity that it admits of no further emphasis, so that this itself was an emphasis through the absence of emphasis, he resumed the report about what he had informed them needs no oath, by affirming the emphatic particle on account of their denial, so that the speech would combine emphasis by negation with emphasis by affirmation. So he said: ﴿Indeed it﴾, i.e., this which the surah of "Nun" concluded with, and which indicated the Hour through these methods it brought, which, along with being wise and miraculous, ﴿is the word﴾, i.e., the recitation, ﴿of a Messenger﴾, i.e., I sent him and it is taken from Me, and there is nothing in it from his own self; rather, all of it is a message that is very clear, and I bear witness to it with the miraculous quality it possesses, which testifies that it is My speech.

And since it is the nature of a Messenger not to convey except what his Sender sent him with, and since some messengers may have added or subtracted, deliberately or by forgetfulness, He informed that the Prophet ﷺ had from the attribute that would preserve him, so He said: ﴿noble﴾, i.e., he is in the utmost degree of nobility (karam), which is distance from the blemishes of character by displaying its excellences, due to the nobility of the soul and the nobility of his forefathers; so he neither adds nor subtracts. And "karuma al-shay'" means the gathering of the perfections fitting to it within it.

(p-376) When He, glorified and exalted be He, established that it is the word of His Messenger (ﷺ), who speaks to us, and it is a revelation (hawl) that does not speak from desire, He negated of it what they fabricate against it. He began with poetry, which is what a person says of his own accord in a deliberate meter, whether truthful or false. Poetry, for its restriction to meter and rhyme, necessarily involves a kind of artifice (takalluf), from which the Qur'an is far removed. It shares with rhymed prose (saj') that artifice, which falls short of the meaning, but it surpasses saj' in meter, which lends it brilliance (rawnaq) and sweetness. So He said: ﴿And it is not﴾, i.e., this Reminder [in its inner reality or its outward form], ﴿the word of a poet﴾. He emphasized the negation, saying: ﴿the word of a poet﴾, i.e., one who brings speech that is rhymed and metered with the intention of meter. It was said that it is not the word of one who is like that because such a person's speech accords with meter only in rare places relative to the whole of the Qur'an. It is certain that no poet would accept that, namely that he would set himself up in the position of versifying and bind himself to the obligation of meter, and then produce speech most of which is unmetered. Thus it is known with certainty that what happened to accord with meter in it was unintended, and so it is not poetry.

Since the Qur'an's divergence from poetry is hidden, in that only poets know this and they are few among people, while most do not know it, He concluded the verse with faith, which is affirmation of the unseen, saying, exalted be He: ﴿Little is it that you believe﴾, i.e., you bring about affirmation, which is faith, only to a small degree or for a short time. That is because I have informed you of this in more than one place, yet you did not believe, although among you are many poets who know with complete knowledge that it differs from poetry. Some of them informed you of this, such as al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah and others, yet you did not follow that with its fruit, which is faith in Allah and His Messenger. Their little faith was the acknowledgment of whichever of their poets acknowledged that it is not poetry, and their sincerity toward the Oneness (wahdaniyyah) at times of necessity, and their singling out of the Creator for creation and lordship. This is a linguistic faith (imān lughawī), not a legal one (lā sharʿī),

Since the Prophet ﷺ was known to be a poet, and whoever knows poetry also knows prose, and prose is the higher of the two, He placed poetry first and then followed it with prose, saying: ﴿nor the word of a soothsayer﴾. The soothsayer (kahin) is the astrologer (munajjim) who reports things that he makes others imagine to a spirit (ra'i) that informs him of them. Most of what he says has no validity, and he expresses this in deliberately contrived rhymed prose (saj') (saj' is rhymed prose in which the meaning follows the wording, for the sake of ornamenting the sound through matching final syllables).

Since the difference between the Qur'an and saj' is very subtle, given that the Qur'an largely consists of verse-endings (fawasil), and because it omits them in the verse of resurrection, the difference is clear. Rhymed-prose writers do not accept bringing a closing rhyme that has no partner, and they consider that a defective and bad flaw (wa'y, 'ayb). Likewise, lengthening one rhymed unit beyond its counterpart, or making it weaker than its equal, is something no rhymed-prose writer would accept, even if he were asleep.

The Prophet's ﷺ separation from the soothsayers is very clear. The soothsayer is one who sets himself up to point out lost things and to report unseen matters, sometimes being correct and often lying. He takes a fee for this and limits himself to whoever asks him. Therefore He described them with "kahin" and not "sajī'". He directed the matter toward reflection, saying: ﴿Little do you remember﴾. He emphasised the matter of scarcity and obscurity by merging the taa' of the tafa''ul form (تَذَكَّرُونَ, tadhakkarūn, which is written with the taa' of the tafa''ul pattern assimilated into the dhāl as tadhdhakarūn) into the following letter, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿you remember﴾. Therefore the matter is confused for you, or for those upon whom you confuse it. He knew that what distinguishes between the two exists among them, because He sees that the Book follows the sound, established meaning. If it is perfectly sound, together with matching rhyme-letter counterparts, then it stands; otherwise it moves away from that to rhyme-endings that do not match in the rhyme letter (rawiyy), nor anything close to it, or to an isolated unit that could be made like the preceding one, but with a deficiency in the restricted form, excess length of speech, and the like.

The Prophet ﷺ never, on any day, claimed knowledge of the unseen, nor claimed any share of his noble self in anything that soothsayers claim. He never related from the jinn any report which he claimed to have derived from them, nor did he praise them for that as soothsayers do. Rather, he condemned the wicked among them in the strongest terms, and said: "Most of what they bring is falsehood." He never asked a fee for what he called people to, nor limited himself to those who came to him asking. Rather, he ﷺ would follow people into their gatherings, calling them to God by rescuing them from error. Therefore his separation from the soothsayers requires nothing beyond a little reflection, as the merging of the taa' of the tafa''ul form indicates. Thus it is established that the speech is not soothsaying, and its speaker and its conveyer is not a soothsayer. And attributing the speech to the one who conveys it, because he is the conveyer, is clearly correct.

(p-379) When He had established that it is the word of the Messenger who does not speak from desire, and negated what might be confused with poetry and soothsaying, and did not mention what they used to accuse him of, namely sorcery and "confused dreams," because that is a pure matter of which no one has doubt, and since the surah was intended to establish the realities that may be hidden, He described it with what confirms what was intended about its attribution to the Messenger (ﷺ), saying: ﴿A revelation﴾ [i.e.] in the manner of gradual sending down, and He indicated its sending to all creation, of the people of the heavens and the earth, by His saying: ﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾, i.e. its Originator and Regulator, who manages them with kindness toward them, according to what each of them understands from this Reminder with which He nurtured them. And Glorified is He, He arranged its composition in a manner that made easy for each of them something that suffices for their explanatory guidance, unlike poetry and soothsaying, for only a few people understand them, not all the worlds. Rather, many of the great scholars and the most skilled among them, perhaps, when a poem from the poems of the Arabs is read to one of them now, does not understand its intended meaning and it does not become clear to him in any way.

In the commentary of al-Biqa'i, *Nazm al-Durar*:

Since there remains among the categories of the claims that they would make against him, the fabrication in the matter of the messengership, in the sense that he came upon some of the books of God Most High that were revealed to the prophets before him, peace be upon them, and appropriated them without any revelation being made to him, and since the evidence that this is not so is that custom rules out that any person among the people would become aware of something that none of them had become aware of, [and -] especially if that person had little contact with the scholars, how much more so if he was unlettered (*ummi*, one who neither writes nor reads), as he (ﷺ) was. He said, linking it to what is implied by its estimate: "If the Revelation of the Lord of the worlds had not come to him, they would not have been able to match it," ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings﴾, that is, had he burdened himself to say, once in a while, a lie ﴿against Us﴾, concerning what We possess of attributes of greatness, majesty, splendour, perfection and magnificence ﴿some sayings﴾ that We had not said, or that We had said but had not permitted him to say.
